instructions: Start the rice first. Rinse 1 1/2 cups of short-grain rice and cook it the way the package says.

Slice the cod 1/2 inch thick on a slight angle into pieces about 2 inches long. Pat them dry with paper towels and lay them on a plate. Sprinkle 3/4 tsp of the salt over both sides and let them sit for 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the dipping sauce. In a small bowl, stir 3 tbsp soy sauce, 2 tbsp rice vinegar, 2 tbsp water, the sesame oil and the sugar until the sugar dissolves. Put the gochugaru in its own small bowl for the table.
Put the flour on a large plate. Crack the eggs into a shallow bowl, add the remaining 1/4 tsp salt and beat them with a fork until no streaks of white are left.
Heat a large nonstick skillet over medium-low heat with 3 tbsp of the oil for 1 minute. Dredge half the cod in the flour and shake off the extra. Dip each piece in the egg so it's coated all over.
Lay the coated pieces in the skillet in a single layer. Cook for 3 minutes, until the underside is pale gold. Don't turn the heat up. The egg should stay light, not dark brown.
Flip the pieces and cook the other side for 2 to 3 minutes. The fish is done when it flakes if you press a piece with a fork. Transfer to a plate.
Wipe the skillet with a paper towel, add the remaining 3 tbsp oil and repeat with the rest of the cod.
Taste a piece. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Serve with the rice and the dipping sauce, with the gochugaru on the side for the adults.
method_notes: Every version is the same idea: salt thin slices of white fish, flour, then egg, then pan-fry gently so the egg stays pale. The lead (Food Network Kitchen) fries 3 to 4 minutes a side over medium-low and uses a soy and vinegar dipping sauce; Korea Times and Easy Korean Food use less egg and shorter times, and Korea Times adds sesame oil to the sauce, which I kept. No page for this dish shows 20 or more ratings (Food Network Kitchen shows none), so the lead is the best-read version and it is a fallback. Gochugaru is on the side so the base stays mild.
